name: Take control
summary: A unit takes over an enemy so that it fights for the other side. The takeover comes from a psychic shot, a held link, a planted parasite or a hack, and hands over the whole victim. Many hold one victim at a time. Most keep their captives until the controller dies; some convert them for good, even past the controller's death, and a few are timed or snap when the victim strays too far; some seize a whole group for a short while. Controllers are usually poor fighters themselves, and whole kinds of target are immune: crewless machines against the psychic kind, living units against the hacking kind, and often heroes and aircraft. Stealing a vehicle by removing its crew is hijack a vehicle; making enemies attack each other without commanding them is confuse enemies.
counterplay: Kill the controller: in nearly every version its death frees the victim at once, and controllers tend to be fragile or unarmed.
Break the link before or after it locks: leave its range or line of sight, or shake it off (hold F in the player version).
Field units it cannot take: crewless robots and drones against psychic control, soldiers against a hacker, and aircraft or heroes where the game makes them immune.
Send cheap units in first and keep valuable ones back: a controller that holds one victim at a time is used up on the first unit it takes.
Spread out, so a captured unit has no friends within reach, and keep a teammate ready to disable or finish the captive.
Outrange it: most links reach only medium range, so long-range fire kills the controller before it can lock on.

other_examples.note: The clone holds one victim at a time and the tower up to three; both keep their captives until they are destroyed (the tower also lets go when its power runs low), and the captives then return to their owners. Miners, dogs, heroes, psychic units, robots and fliers cannot be taken, and nobody can steal a unit that another controller already holds. Captives are often marched straight into a recycling building.

other_examples.unit: Mastermind (Scrin), Cultists and Prodigy (Traveler-59, Kane's Wrath)
other_examples.note: Here control is an ability on a cooldown, not a main attack. The Mastermind commando takes one unit or even a building and can then withdraw; each Cultist squad holds one victim and loses it on taking another or on dying, but squads have no build limit, so many of them add up. The Prodigy adds a timed takeover of every ground unit in an area, and once it has a victim the link holds from anywhere on the map. Commandos, epic units and fliers resist.

Takes one enemy unit for a short, fixed time; the unit keeps its upgrades and abilities. Control returns early if the infestor dies or the victim gets a few spaces further away than the cast range. Heroic units are immune, and loaded transports cannot be taken.

sources.title: Neural Parasite ability box, StarCraft Wiki

other_examples.note: A permanent takeover of any enemy unit that stays with the new owner even after the dark archon dies. Each cast drains all of the caster's shields, leaving it exposed, and taking a transport brings its passengers along.

sources.title: Mind Control ability box (StarCraft), StarCraft Wiki

other_examples.note: A slow, unarmed monk converts one enemy unit at a time from range to its own side, then has to rest while its faith refills; the player must order every conversion by hand. Scout cavalry resist it and hunt monks, research lets monks convert siege engines and buildings, and one defensive technology makes a converted unit die instead of changing sides.

sources.title: Monk (Age of Empires II), Age of Empires Series Wiki
Conversion, Age of Empires Series Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: A defender fires small hacking robots onto an attacker's drone, or plants them where a drone will pass; the hack takes a few seconds, a planted pest warns nearby drones, and then the defender drives the drone as his own while the attacker loses it. Only drones can be taken, and EMP grenades, electronics detectors and drone lasers deal with pests and hacked drones.

A pilot holds the action key behind an enemy Spectre robot to rewrite it, and other Spectres close by switch sides too; the pilot can't fight back during the hack. In one co-op mode the number of hacked Spectres is capped at five.

Turns one enemy into a thrall that fights for the players and spreads the effect to the enemies it hits. Thralls last a set time, only seven may exist at once, and a radiation effect turns them back for a while.

A top-down hero takes control of neutral or enemy creeps, never heroes, and keeps them until they die; the number he may keep grows with the ability's level, and persuading one more than that kills the oldest at once.

player_translation.summary: A fragile controller that holds a link on one enemy. After a short, visible wind-up it takes the victim's weapon for a few seconds: you aim and fire their gun at their own team while they keep moving and struggle to shake you off. Only things no player drives, such as a turret or a summoned beast, stay yours until you die.
as_user: You buy a T2 or T3 support unit with little or no gun of its own; your worth is what you take.

Hold the link on an enemy within medium range. It builds for a moment and fails if you lose line of sight or take a heavy hit. Once it locks, your cursor aims the victim's weapon and your fire button fires it, while you stand still and your own gun is silent.
Choose victims for their guns: a heavy tank in the middle of its escort, a rocket soldier beside friendly vehicles. Kills made with a captured weapon are yours.
One victim at a time: control lasts a few seconds or until they shake free, and a new link drops the old one. Something no player drives (an enemy turret, a summoned beast) stays yours until you die.
Immune targets carry an icon and refuse the link from the start, so you learn to pick your fights.
as_target: The wind-up shows: a beam from the controller and a rising tone. Break line of sight, dash away or burst the controller before it locks.

Once taken you keep your movement and lose your gun: the HUD says 'weapon hijacked', a ring in the enemy's colour circles your unit and an arrow points at the controller. Turn so your muzzle points away from your teammates.
Hold F to struggle free; the bar fills faster while your team hurts the controller. In a vehicle you can also hold X to bail out and deny the gun.
When it ends you are immune to control for a short time, so nobody can chain-control you.
teammates: The victim's team shoots the controller (heavy damage breaks the link), steps out of the hijacked gun's line and brings immune units to hunt it.
The controller's team escorts it, because it can barely fight, and sets up targets: a puller drags a tank into link range, a stun holds it still for the wind-up.
A hijacked weapon hurts its own team, the one exception to the usual friendly-fire rules, so both teams must be able to see it.
controls: Move with WASD and aim with the mouse.

Hold right mouse on an enemy in range to start the link. Once locked, the mouse aims the victim's weapon and left mouse fires it; release right mouse to let go early. One counted key, within the T2 budget.
Victim, with the universal keys: hold F to break free; hold X to bail out of a vehicle.
feedback: A pulsing link line in the controller's colour from controller to victim, readable from above.
The victim's outline and nameplate switch to the controller's colour with rippling rings over it, as Red Alert 2 marks controlled units.
A pulse sound when the link locks and a ringing tone when it breaks (both used in Red Alert 2), plus an announcer line for the victim's team.
A small anti-control icon on immune units and a cooldown ring under the controller.
The kill feed shows the controller's icon next to kills made with a captured weapon.
changes_from_rts: RTS control hands over full command until the controller dies; against a person that takes them out of the game, so here only the weapon is taken, for a few seconds, and the victim can always move and struggle.
RTS controllers fire on their own at anything in reach; here the player picks, aims and holds the link, and the wind-up gives the target a reaction window.
Red Alert 2 players often walk captives into a recycling building; recycling another player is not acceptable, so player captives are only borrowed.
Permanent conversion (Brood War, Age of Empires) is kept only for things no player drives.
Immunities stay, but they must be visible: from above, players need an icon to know that a drone or a hero can't be taken.
Add a short immunity after control ends and a one-link rule, so a controller can't keep one player locked down.
The captured weapon must take the controller's aim from the server, with lag compensation, or shots will feel wrong to both players.

team_play.notes: The controller needs an escort and a setup (a pull or a stun); the victim's team needs immune picks, spacing and someone to break the link by shooting the controller.

notes: Routing one player's weapon to another player's aim and trigger, with the server in charge, is new plumbing.
A friendly-fire exception for captured weapons, plus kill credit and assists for captured fire.
Edge cases: the victim dies, switches seats, boards or leaves a vehicle or teleports; the controller dies mid-link; two controllers try the same victim (the first link wins, as in Red Alert 2).
Immunity rules by nature and class across every unit, and UI on both sides (wind-up, link line, struggle bar).
Turning the enemy's best weapon on its own team is a big swing; duration, wind-up and the immunity window are the levers.
Chained control by several controllers can lock one player out of the fight; one link per victim and a post-control immunity prevent it.
A controller hiding behind cover and fighting with a captured tank takes no risk, so the link needs line of sight and roots the controller.
Immune classes can become mandatory picks once controllers are common.
Everyone must tell a hijacked ally from an enemy at a glance.
In a crowded fight it must stay clear who is linked to whom.
A friendly tank shooting you is confusing unless the colour switch is unmistakable.

variants.name: Weapon puppet
variants.summary: Takes only the victim's weapon for a few seconds; the victim keeps moving and can shake free. The default against players.
variants.seen_in: A player-safe cut of Red Alert 2 and StarCraft II control; infest-vehicle's latched-control variant does the same from on board

variants.name: Lasting link
variants.summary: Control lasts until the controller dies, one victim at a time, and taking a new one frees the old. On players it is capped at the base duration; it lasts only on things no player drives.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Yuri Clone, Tiberium Wars Mastermind, Kane's Wrath Cultists

variants.name: Machine hack
variants.summary: A tech version that takes only crewless machines (drones, turrets, robots) after a short, warned hack; living units are immune. It turns the psychic immunity inside out.
variants.seen_in: Rainbow Six Siege Mozzie, Titanfall data knife

counters.why: Enemy drones, turrets and robots become its own.

countered_by.why: Soldiers and beasts have nothing to hack and can shoot the hacker during its wind-up.
EMP knocks out the hacking device and the machines it has taken.

variants.name: Leashed parasite
variants.summary: A parasite shot gives full control of one enemy for a short, fixed time; it ends early if the controller dies or the victim is taken too far away.

variants.name: Auto-capture field
variants.summary: Passive: enemies are taken one after another as they enter range, with no order needed and no way to hold back. Pairs with overload past a safe limit.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Mastermind and Psychic Tower

variants.name: Pay per capture
variants.summary: Each capture costs the controller something large, such as its whole shield or a long rest, so it must be protected after every take.
variants.seen_in: Brood War dark archon (loses its shields), Age of Empires II monk (must regain faith)

variants.name: Spreading thralls
variants.summary: Captives pass the control on to the enemies they hit, up to a small total, for a set time.

variants.name: Area seizure
variants.summary: An ultimate that briefly seizes every non-immune ground enemy in an area.

adds_strengths.why: Turns an enemy's own weapon against its team for a few seconds, so the enemy's best gun becomes its problem.

adds_weaknesses.why: Stands still and silent while it holds a link, has little firepower of its own, and immune targets ignore it.

counters.why: A heavy vehicle in the middle of its escort is the best prize: its gun turns on its own side.
Armour does not stop the link, so the toughest units are as easy to take as the weakest.

countered_by.why: Crewless machines are immune to psychic control and can hunt the controller freely.
Fliers stay out of most links' reach and pick off the slow controller.
Long-range fire kills the controller before its medium-range link can lock.

open_questions: Against players, should control take only the weapon (as proposed here) or movement too, and for how long?
Should a hijacked weapon hurt its own team even in modes without friendly fire?
Which units are immune in Shamble Frontlines: crewless machines (psychic kind), living units (hacking kind), and are heroes and aircraft immune as well?
Should lasting control of turrets and summons exist at all, or is every capture timed?

shooter_fit.reason: Taking over a person's unit is frustrating, so it only works cut down to a short weapon hijack with a wind-up and a struggle; Rainbow Six Siege shows that the machine-only version works between players.
